turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hi, Dr. [Name]. I, uh... I guess I'm here because things have just gotten really overwhelming lately. I mean, they've always been a bit chaotic, but recently it's just... it's too much. I'm a software developer, right? But I also do all these other things. I've got patent notes I need to review, and I'm supposed to be prepping for this workshop, plus there are these gallery deadlines for my wife that I promised I'd help manage, and on top of all that, there are all these team decisions at work that I have to sign off on. 

And the thing is, I just can't seem to organize all these moving parts anymore. It's like I have all these tabs open in my brain, and I can't figure out which one I'm supposed to be looking at. So instead of sitting down and prioritizing what actually matters—like the things that are really going to move the needle or the things that have actual, hard deadlines—I just end up starting whatever is loudest. You know? Like, whatever email just popped up, or whoever is pinging me on Slack right that second, or whatever random thought just crossed my mind. And then the important stuff just sits there, piling up, and I get more and more stressed out about it, but I still can't seem to just organize it and get it done. It's exhausting, honestly. I just feel like I'm constantly putting out fires instead of actually building anything.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they cannot organize the moving parts of their life and struggle to prioritize tasks, instead reacting to whatever is 'loudest'.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli like pop-up emails, Slack pings, and random thoughts.

turns.doctor_question: Over the past few weeks or months, have you noticed periods where your mood felt consistently low, sad, or irritable—not just stressed about the work chaos, but a deeper kind of mood change that lasted for days or longer?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, it's not like a dark cloud or anything like that. I don't wake up feeling sad or hopeless, you know? It's really just... well, it's entirely tied to whatever disaster I'm currently trying to manage. 

Like, if I realize I completely forgot to send the finalized specs to the QA team and they've been waiting on me all morning, yeah, I get incredibly irritated with myself. I'll sit there and think, "Come on, how did you drop the ball on this again?" But it doesn't linger for days in this deep, heavy way. It's more of a sharp, intense frustration right in the moment. And then, you know, an hour later I might actually figure out a really elegant solution to a completely different coding problem, or I'll stumble across this fascinating new framework I want to look into, and suddenly I'm feeling totally fine, even energized! 

So my mood bounces around a lot based on what I'm doing, or, well, what I'm failing to do, I guess. But it's never that sustained, deep sadness you're talking about. My wife actually asked me something similar a few weeks ago when I was tearing my hair out over her gallery logistics—she was worried I was getting depressed because I was being so short with her. But I told her, and I really believe this, it's not sadness. It's just... I'm just so annoyed that my brain won't cooperate with me. If the work was actually handled and the plates weren't all spinning out of control, I'd be perfectly happy. It's not a mood thing, it's just a constant reaction to the chaos.

symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions completely forgetting to send finalized specs to the QA team, indicating forgetfulness in daily work activities.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies experiencing sustained, deep sadness or waking up feeling sad.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient describes still finding things fascinating and feeling energized by new coding frameworks, denying a loss of interest.
symptom_reasoning.S083: The patient explicitly states they do not wake up feeling hopeless.

turns.doctor_question: Going back to when you were in school or early in your career—would you say you've always had this trouble with organization and staying focused on priorities, or is this something that's gotten noticeably worse recently?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've actually been thinking a lot about this lately. My wife and I were going through some old boxes in the attic last month—we were looking for this specific set of tax documents from like five years ago, which of course I had misplaced, which is a whole other story—but anyway, we ended up finding this box of my old school stuff that my mom had saved. And I was looking through some of my old report cards from elementary school, like third and fourth grade, right? 

And it was honestly kind of a revelation. Because, you know, I always thought of myself as just being a bit scattered now because adult life is so complicated. But looking at those report cards... it was all right there. Every single teacher wrote the exact same thing. They'd say, "He's a very bright boy, he understands the material," but then there would always be this "but." "But he spends half the class daydreaming," or "He stares out the window during math." And the really crazy part, the part that actually made me laugh out loud when I read it, was how many times they mentioned me losing things. I mean, apparently, I was notorious for doing my homework—like, actually sitting at the kitchen table and finishing it—and then completely forgetting to turn it in. Or I'd just lose the entire homework folder between my house and the classroom. 

So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing. It was happening way back in grade school, long before I even hit my teenage years or had any real responsibilities. I guess I just managed to scrape by because I was smart enough to ace the tests even if I lost the homework, you know? But the underlying issue, that inability to just keep track of things and stay focused on what I'm supposed to be doing... yeah, that's been there pretty much my whole life, as far back as I can see. It's just that now, losing a homework folder is one thing, but dropping the ball on a major software release or my wife's gallery deadlines... the stakes are just so much higher, so it feels a lot worse. But the pattern? The pattern has always been there.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a lifelong inability to stay focused on what they are supposed to be doing.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions failing to turn in completed homework in school and dropping the ball on major work projects as an adult.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient notes an ongoing inability to keep track of things and manage complex adult responsibilities.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly mentions a history of losing things, including tax documents recently and homework folders during childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient recalls teachers noting that they spent half the class daydreaming or staring out the window.

turns.doctor_question: When you're trying to focus on something—whether it's back in school or even now at work—do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, tapping your fingers or feet, or feeling like you need to move around? Or is it more that your mind wanders, but your body is still?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's... it's actually a bit of both, I think, but the physical part is definitely there, and it can be really intense. I mean, it's incredibly noticeable to me, especially nowadays with how much time we spend on video conferences. We have these incredibly long design calls at work—sometimes they stretch for two, maybe even two and a half hours when we're trying to map out the architecture for a new software release or hash out the backend logic. And because I'm one of the senior devs, I'm expected to be present, on camera, and looking completely dialed in, right? 

But the reality is, after maybe twenty or thirty minutes, I start feeling this... this actual pressure building up in my body. It's hard to explain if you haven't felt it, but it's just this intense, physical need to get up. It’s almost like a coil tightening inside my chest and my legs. So what I end up doing is, well, I'll literally pace around my home office. Sometimes I'll make up an excuse to turn my camera off for a quick second—like pretending my connection is unstable—just so I can walk circles around the room and burn off that tension. 

And even when the camera has to stay on, and I'm really trying my absolute hardest to look totally focused on whoever is sharing their screen, I'm just constantly moving. I'll shift my weight back and forth, or I'll actually swap seats entirely. I have my regular ergonomic desk chair, but I also have this taller drafting stool over in the corner, and I'll find myself literally shifting from chair to chair throughout the call just to do *something* with that physical energy. It takes so much effort just to sit there and look like a normal, attentive person when inside my body is just screaming at me to get up and move. So, yeah, my mind definitely wanders a lot, like I mentioned with the daydreaming back in school, but my body is absolutely not still. Not at all.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states that their mind wanders a lot.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes constantly moving and shifting their weight back and forth while trying to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions leaving their seat to pace around the room or swap chairs during video calls where they are expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense physical pressure and need to get up and move, indicating severe internal restlessness.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever noticed periods where you needed significantly less sleep than usual—like feeling fully rested after just a few hours—and during those times you had a lot more energy and were able to accomplish more than normal, even if it only lasted a few days?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, no. No, definitely not. Sleep is... well, I mean, I am very much someone who needs their sleep. Actually, it's kind of a running joke with my wife, because in my line of work—software development, especially when we're pushing a major release or doing a massive server migration—there's this whole industry culture of pulling all-nighters. You know, that classic stereotype of the coder fueled by energy drinks and pizza at three in the morning, just hacking away. 

And sure, I've had to do that a few times when things were completely on fire and we had a hard deadline the next morning. Like, just last year, we had this catastrophic database issue right before a big client launch, and I was up until maybe four in the morning writing hotfixes and trying to patch the leaks. But the thing is, the next day? I was absolutely useless. I mean, completely wrecked. I didn't feel energized or fully rested at all, not even a little bit. My brain felt like it was stuffed with wet cotton, and I think I drank about four cups of coffee just to keep my eyes open and physically upright during the post-mortem meeting. I was dragging for the rest of the week, honestly. 

So, no, if I only get a few hours of sleep, I feel it. I feel it really hard. I never have those periods where I just magically don't need sleep and feel amazing or super productive. If anything, my usual scatteredness—the dropping the ball on things, the losing my train of thought—that all gets ten times worse if I don't get at least seven, preferably eight hours. My wife always tells me I turn into a complete zombie if I try to skimp on rest, so I really try to avoid it whenever possible. Even if my mind is sort of spinning at night thinking about a piece of code I can't figure out, I know I have to force myself to sleep because I'll pay for it otherwise. So I definitely don't have those days where I'm surviving on three hours and conquering the world. It's just not how my system works at all.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions 'dropping the ball on things' as part of their usual behavior, implying difficulty following through on tasks or responsibilities.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient refers to their 'usual scatteredness' and 'losing my train of thought', indicating ongoing difficulties with concentration.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies having periods of feeling 'amazing or super productive' or 'conquering the world' on little sleep.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient strongly denies ever needing significantly less sleep, stating they feel 'completely wrecked' and 'useless' if they don't get enough rest.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had times—maybe lasting a few days or a week—where your thoughts felt like they were racing or jumping from one thing to another much faster than usual, or where you felt like you could take on way more projects than you normally would, even though you knew logically it might be too much?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think about that for a second. I mean, it's a little tricky to answer because my thoughts are always kind of bouncing around a bit, right? Like I was saying earlier about the daydreaming, my brain is always sort of wandering off. I'll be looking at a block of code and suddenly I'm thinking about whether I remembered to pay the water bill, or I'm wondering what my wife is planning for her gallery exhibit. But it doesn't feel... it doesn't feel like a high-speed train or anything. It's not like my brain suddenly goes into overdrive for a week. It's more just my normal, everyday level of distraction. It's like being in a room where a few too many radios are playing at a normal volume, rather than one radio suddenly blasting at double speed, if that makes sense.

And as for taking on way more projects... honestly, that is pretty much the exact opposite of how I operate. I actually have a really, really hard time just managing the projects I already have on my plate. Like, right now at work, we're in the middle of this massive migration to AWS, and my manager, Dave—who is a great guy, don't get me wrong, but he's very ambitious—he's always trying to hand out these side initiatives. Just last Tuesday we had our one-on-one, and he asked if I wanted to spearhead the new mentorship program for the junior developers this quarter. And I just looked at him like he had two heads, because I can barely keep my own Jira tickets organized as it is! 

I'm constantly feeling like I'm just barely treading water with my baseline expectations, trying not to drop the ball on the things I'm already committed to. So the idea of suddenly waking up one day and feeling this... this surge of confidence, or feeling invincible and volunteering for five new things because I think I can handle it all? Yeah, no, that just doesn't happen to me. I know there are guys in the tech industry who operate like that—you know, the stereotypical "10x developers" who will suddenly get inspired and rewrite an entire legacy codebase over a long weekend—but that is definitely not me. I never get those periods where I feel superhuman or like I can take on the world. I'm just trying to get through my normal to-do list without losing my notes.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient states he has a really hard time managing his current projects and can barely keep his work tickets organized.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions trying to get through his to-do list 'without losing my notes,' implying a tendency to lose items.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes his brain constantly wandering off to unrelated thoughts, characterizing it as his 'normal, everyday level of distraction.'
symptom_reasoning.S035: The patient explicitly denies ever feeling a surge of confidence, feeling invincible, or feeling superhuman.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient denies experiencing periods where his thoughts feel like a high-speed train or go into overdrive.
symptom_reasoning.S040: The patient denies taking on way more projects or volunteering for new things, stating it is the exact opposite of how he operates.

turns.doctor_question: Going back to those old report cards and your elementary school years, did your teachers ever mention anything about you talking too much in class, interrupting other kids, or having trouble waiting your turn? Or did your parents ever notice you being particularly impulsive or acting without thinking?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, definitely not. If anything, they probably wished I talked a little bit more. I was... well, I was the exact opposite of that kid. I actually remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins—or wait, maybe it was Mrs. Gable? No, it was Mrs. Higgins, because she was the one who taught math, which you'd think I would have been super engaged in since I eventually went into software architecture and computer science. But she actually pulled my mother aside at a parent-teacher conference once. I think it was right around Thanksgiving break, and she told my mom that I was basically like a ghost in the classroom. 

I never raised my hand, and I absolutely never blurted out answers. If she actually called on me, it would usually take me a good ten seconds just to figure out what page we were on, or even what subject we were doing, because I was completely zoned out, staring out the window or drawing these incredibly intricate little mazes in the margins of my notebooks. Which, honestly, is kind of funny when you think about it now—mapping out mazes is pretty much what I do with backend server routing today. But anyway, no, interrupting other kids or having trouble waiting my turn? Never. I was way too stuck in my own head to even notice what the other kids were doing, let alone interrupt them. I was always the kid at the back of the line for recess just kind of shuffling along, completely lost in thought.

And as for my parents... no, they never saw me as impulsive or acting without thinking, either. My older brother, Mark, now *he* was the impulsive one. He was always breaking things, jumping off the roof of the garage, getting into trouble, and my parents were constantly having to chase him around and put out fires. With me, they always just said I was "in my own little world." My mom used to call me her little absent-minded professor. I'd walk into the kitchen and just stand there in the middle of the room, having completely forgotten why I went in there in the first place, or I'd leave my lunchbox on the roof of my mom's car. But I never acted without thinking. Honestly, if anything, I overthought things until I just drifted off before I could even make a decision. So, yeah, none of that disruptive, hyperactive stuff. No talking out of turn. I was just quietly missing absolutely everything that was going on around me.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes being so zoned out that when called upon by the teacher, it took him ten seconds to figure out what was going on.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes being constantly lost in thought, stuck in his own head, and staring out the window instead of paying attention.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes forgetting why he walked into a room and leaving his lunchbox on the roof of the car.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies having any 'disruptive, hyperactive stuff'.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient denies talking too much, stating his teachers probably wished he talked more.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states he 'absolutely never blurted out answers'.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly denies ever having trouble waiting his turn.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies ever interrupting other kids.

turns.doctor_question: When you do manage to sit down and actually start working on something—like one of those important tasks you mentioned—how long can you typically stay focused on it before your attention drifts away, or before you feel the urge to switch to something else?
turns.patient_response:
Well, gosh, how long... you know, I really couldn't give you a specific number on that. I've honestly never timed it, and it’s—it’s so hard to quantify because it’s not like a timer goes off in my head. I mean, I’ll sit down at my desk, right? And I have this whole setup process to try and force myself into the zone. I get my coffee—always in this specific insulated mug my wife got me so it stays hot, because otherwise I forget about it and it goes cold—and I put on my noise-canceling headphones. I usually put on some kind of instrumental synthwave, something without lyrics so it doesn't mess with my internal monologue. I open up my development environment on my main monitor, maybe pull up some AWS documentation on the left screen, and I tell myself, "Okay, we are going to knock out this API integration right now." 

And I start. I really do. But then... I don't know, I really have no idea how long it is before I drift. It could be five minutes, it could be fifteen? I just don't know. Because I don't usually feel this conscious urge to switch tasks. It’s not like I’m sitting there actively thinking, "Oh, I’m bored, I want to go look at something else." It’s much more insidious than that. 

Like, I’ll be typing out a function, and I’ll need to name a variable. And I’ll think, "Wait, did we use camel case or snake case for the database schema on this particular microservice?" So I open up another file just to check the schema. But while I'm in that file, I see a comment left by a developer, Greg, who actually left the company like two years ago to work at a startup in Austin. Which then reminds me that my brother-in-law was talking about moving to Austin, and I wonder what the housing market is like down there right now. 

So then I open a new browser tab just to do a quick Zillow search, just out of curiosity, you know? And suddenly it’s forty-five minutes later, I’ve got twelve tabs open about Texas property taxes and the best barbecue joints in Travis County, and my code is just sitting there in the background, completely untouched. So, yeah, I really couldn't tell you how long the actual focus lasts before the drift happens. It slips away so quietly, and so naturally, that I don't even notice I've stopped working until I'm already miles down some completely unrelated rabbit hole. So I really don't have a good answer for the exact timing of it, unfortunately. It just sort of... evaporates.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to maintain focus on work tasks for more than 5 to 15 minutes before drifting away and leaving the work untouched.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient provides a clear example of being easily distracted by a chain of unrelated thoughts (a coworker, a brother-in-law, the Austin housing market) that completely derails their work.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever been formally evaluated or diagnosed with ADHD, or has anyone—a doctor, psychologist, or school—ever suggested that might be something to look into?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, never. I've never been formally evaluated for anything like this. And honestly, no one—no teacher, no doctor, nobody—ever suggested I look into it either. 

I think a lot of that just comes down to the timing of when I grew up, you know? I was in elementary school in the early to mid-eighties, and back then, they really only noticed the kids who were literally bouncing off the walls or throwing erasers across the room. Like I was saying earlier, since I was just quietly staring out the window or drawing my little mazes, I wasn't a problem for the teachers. I wasn't disrupting the lesson, so why would they send me to the school psychologist, right? They just labeled me a daydreamer, maybe told my mom I needed to apply myself more, and moved on. 

And then, as I got older, I think I just managed to fly under the radar because I got decent grades. I mean, I got through college, I even got a master's degree, which sounds great on paper. But the reality behind the scenes was just a nightmare of getting completely distracted for weeks, and then having to do everything in a sheer panic at the absolute last minute. I would literally be in the computer lab at 4:00 AM, chugging terrible vending machine coffee, writing an entire architecture paper the morning it was due because I'd spent the previous three weeks going down completely unrelated rabbit holes instead of working on it. But because I always managed to scrape it together and get a B-plus, none of my professors ever pulled me aside to say, "Hey, you seem to be struggling, maybe we should look into this." They just saw the finished product. 

Even my regular doctor—Dr. Aris, who I've been seeing for about ten years now—he's great, but we just talk about standard physical stuff. We talk about my cholesterol, which is actually a little high right now, so I've been trying to eat more oatmeal and cut back on red meat, but we never talk about how my brain works. He checks my blood pressure, asks if I'm exercising, and that's the end of the appointment. Mental focus, memory, how long it takes me to do a simple coding task at work... none of that has ever come up in a medical setting. 

So, yeah, no professional has ever pointed a finger at this. It’s always just been me feeling like I’m pushing a massive boulder up a hill while everyone else is just walking normally, but nobody ever told me there might be a reason for it or suggested I get checked out.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes poor time management and organization, noting they had to do everything in a sheer panic at the absolute last minute.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly mentions getting completely distracted for weeks and going down completely unrelated rabbit holes instead of working.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient notes they were quietly staring out the window or drawing mazes, indicating they were capable of engaging in activities quietly.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient contrasts their behavior with kids who were 'bouncing off the walls,' stating they were quiet and not disruptive.
